opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the first thing to say is that the comparison is messier than it looks. People often point out that a kid learns language from maybe tens of millions of words, while these models see trillions of tokens, and conclude humans are something like a thousand or ten thousand times more sample efficient. That's a real gap, but you have to be careful about what you're comparing.

One way I'd frame it is to ask how much of human learning is really "within lifetime" learning, and how much is evolution having already done a big chunk of the search. Evolution ran an enormous optimization process over the architecture, the learning rules, the priors, the developmental schedule. So when a child picks up language quickly, part of that is a very good learning algorithm and part is a strong inductive bias built in. Gradient descent on a transformer starts from close to nothing. So some of the gap is "humans got a huge amount of pretraining for free," and that part isn't really a statement about the learning algorithm being better.

That said, I don't think it explains everything. I'd guess humans really do have a somewhat better learning procedure in some respects. We seem to do something more like active, structured learning: choosing what to attend to, building explicit models, reasoning about why we got something wrong, rehearsing and consolidating. A single gradient step on a token is a pretty dumb update by comparison. It's not deciding what's important; it's just nudging all the weights in the direction that would have made that token slightly more likely.

The way I'd think about it quantitatively is this: there's some gap, maybe a few orders of magnitude, and the question is how fast ML closes it. And I think there are a couple of reasons to expect it to close. Bigger models are already more sample efficient; they learn more per example. And as models get more capable, you can increasingly get the human-like part, the learning that comes from reasoning, reflecting, generating your own training signal, rather than raw gradient updates on external data. In-context learning is already a version of that. It's dramatically more sample efficient than fine-tuning, and it looks a lot more like what a person does when they read something once and get it.

So my overall view is that I wouldn't treat human sample efficiency as a deep barrier. It's more of a hint about where the remaining gains are. It tells you that there exist learning procedures much better than naive SGD on data, which is somewhat of a bullish update on how much room there is, and once systems are smart enough to participate in their own learning, a lot of that gap could close relatively quickly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human learning efficiency and evolution but does not estimate synaptic neuronal firing events using seconds in a human lifetime or the assumption of roughly one event per second.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that the naive comparison is a little misleading, and you have to be careful about what you're actually holding fixed.

So the standard observation is something like: a human sees maybe a hundred million words over the course of their life, and a language model sees trillions, and yet the human ends up pretty competent, so clearly gradient descent is wildly sample inefficient compared to whatever the brain is doing. And I think there's something right about that, but there are a few things that complicate it.

One is that humans aren't starting from scratch. Evolution has done an enormous amount of optimization over the architecture and the learning algorithm and the priors you come in with. So when you ask "how many samples does a human need," you're really asking how many samples does a system need after it's been given a very carefully tuned initialization by a process that itself consumed an astronomical amount of compute and data. If you want an apples-to-apples comparison, you'd want to either count that or think about what happens when you give a neural net a comparably good prior, and we just don't really know how to do that yet.

The second thing is that a lot of the data humans get is much richer than tokens. You're getting continuous sensory input, you're acting in the world and seeing the consequences, you're getting feedback that's targeted at exactly the thing you were confused about. So a "sample" for a human and a "sample" for a model aren't really the same unit. I think when you try to account for bits of information rather than number of examples, the gap shrinks a lot, though I don't think it goes to zero.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most interesting from a forecasting perspective, is that the gap probably does reflect a real algorithmic deficiency, and the question is how big it is and how fast it closes. My guess is that the brain is doing something that's within a few orders of magnitude of what gradient descent does, not something categorically different, and that the remaining gap is the kind of thing that gets eaten over time by better architectures and better ways of structuring the learning problem. I don't think there's a magic ingredient. But I hold that with real uncertainty, and I think it matters a lot for timelines, because if humans are, say, a thousand times more sample efficient and that's fundamentally about the algorithm, then there's a lot of overhang sitting there waiting to be found, and that makes rapid progress more plausible than if we're mostly compute and data constrained.

The way I'd actually try to make progress on it is to look at narrow domains where you can run the comparison cleanly. How quickly does a human learn to play a new game, or learn a new concept from a few examples, versus a model fine-tuned on the same thing? And then try to decompose how much of the human advantage is prior knowledge being transferred versus genuinely faster learning on the new stuff. My impression from that kind of comparison is that the human edge is mostly the prior, and that's a somewhat optimistic story for ML, because priors are the thing scale has been good at buying.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human learning samples, evolution, sensory data, and comparisons with gradient descent, but does not propose estimating neuronal firing events per synapse from the seconds in a human lifetime or assume roughly one event per second.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you’re counting as a sample. A human can see one example of a new task and figure out what to do, but that human has already had an enormous amount of experience. If you compare that to a neural network learning the task from scratch, you’re comparing two pretty different things. The more relevant comparison is to a pretrained model that’s also being shown one example.

There’s also a question about how much of the human advantage comes from evolution. Evolution has done a lot of optimization to produce a brain that learns effectively in the environments humans encounter. It’s hard to know how to account for that computational work, or how much of it is responsible for any particular ability.

So I’d want to distinguish the empirical question—how much experience does a human need to acquire some skill, compared with a model with relevant prior training—from the mechanistic question of whether the brain uses a fundamentally more efficient learning algorithm than gradient descent. You could observe a big difference on the first question without establishing much about the second. The difference could come from the prior, the architecture, or the way experience is collected.

My inclination would be to look at learning in unfamiliar domains, try to make the prior experience as comparable as possible, and see where the gaps remain. I wouldn’t assume that all of human learning is explained by something very much like gradient descent, but I also wouldn’t take humans learning a concept from a few examples as strong evidence against it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses comparing human and model learning experience, but does not propose estimating synaptic firing events from seconds in a human lifetime or assume roughly one event per second.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what we’re counting as a sample. A human can see a few examples of a new task and learn to do it, but they’re bringing an enormous amount of prior experience. So that’s more analogous to taking a pretrained model and giving it a few examples than it is to training a neural network from scratch.

Then there’s a separate question about how efficiently humans acquired all that background knowledge. And there I think the comparison is pretty hard. A human is getting this continuous stream of sensory input, acting in the world, and observing the consequences. If you count each second as one sample, you get a very different impression than if you count all the individual predictions they could be learning from.

The other thing I’d distinguish is gradient descent from the learning algorithm it produces. You could use gradient descent to train a system that, internally, does something much more sophisticated when it encounters a new problem. So observing that a human can reason through something without needing thousands of examples doesn’t by itself establish a limitation of gradient descent. The question is whether gradient descent can produce a system with that ability, and how much training it takes.

I’d probably put the most weight on comparisons where you can make the experience reasonably similar. But even then, if there’s a gap, you have to work out whether it comes from the learning rule, the architecture, the training objective, or the prior knowledge. I don’t think the raw observation that humans learn some tasks from very few examples tells you which of those is responsible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses counting human experience by seconds, but does not propose using a lifetime’s seconds to estimate neuronal firing events encountered by a synapse or state the roughly-one-event-per-second assumption.
